The Pulumi Automation API is a programmatic interface for running Pulumi programs without the Pulumi CLI.

The Pulumi Automation API encapsulates the functionality of the Pulumi CLI (including `pulumi up`, `pulumi preview`, `pulumi destroy`, and `pulumi stack init`) as a strongly typed SDK.
The Pulumi Automation API allows a developer to drive the Pulumi engine from within their own application instead of invoking the `pulumi` command from a shell.
With Automation API you define a Pulumi program, its resources, stacks, and stack configuration entirely in code, then run that code as an ordinary executable in your language of choice.
The page "Using Automation API" at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/automation-api/ provides a step-by-step walkthrough of building an Automation API program.
The page /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/automation-api/#prerequisites provides details on installing the Pulumi CLI for use with Automation API.
The `pulumi api` CLI command can be used to read or modify Pulumi Cloud resources, such as stack metadata, access tokens, or Insights data, without running a Pulumi program.

Automation API is well suited to scenarios where infrastructure provisioning is part of a larger application or workflow, including driving infrastructure deployments within CI/CD workflows, integration testing, multi-stage deployments such as blue-green deployment patterns, deployments involving application code such as database migrations, building higher-level tools such as custom CLIs over Pulumi, exposing Pulumi behind a REST or gRPC API, and debugging Pulumi programs using a single entrypoint with inline programs.
Workspaces manage the execution environment, providing utilities such as plugin installation, environment configuration via `$PULUMI_HOME`, and the creation, deletion, and listing of stacks.
`RemoteWorkspace` represents a workspace for running Pulumi operations remotely with Pulumi Deployments, where the program is located in a remote Git repository.
A `Stack` exposes methods for the full Pulumi lifecycle: `up`, `preview`, `refresh`, and `destroy`, as well as methods for managing configuration.

Automation API can drive two kinds of Pulumi programs: local programs and inline programs.

Unlike traditional Pulumi programs, an inline program doesn't require a separate package on disk with its own file and `Pulumi.yaml`.
Inline programs are functions that can be authored in the same file as your Automation API program or imported from another package.
The inline program's lifecycle must be fully contained within the function, callback, or closure passed as the inline program.

There are three types of functions available in Pulumi programs: provider functions, get functions, and resource methods.
Pulumi provides three types of functions that can be used in Pulumi programs to interact with cloud resources and retrieve data from cloud providers.

Pulumi has dedicated documentation pages for provider functions, get functions, and resource methods at /docs/iac/concepts/functions/provider-functions/, /docs/iac/concepts/functions/get-functions/, and /docs/iac/concepts/functions/resource-methods/ respectively.
Get functions are static methods available on all Pulumi resource classes (in TypeScript, Python, C#, and Java) that allow you to reference an existing resource that is not managed by Pulumi.
Get functions in Go are package-level functions available for all Pulumi resource types that allow you to reference an existing resource that is not managed by Pulumi.
Get functions in Pulumi YAML are available on all Pulumi resource types via the `get:` stanza, allowing you to reference an existing resource that is not managed by Pulumi.
Resources accessed via get functions will never be updated or deleted by Pulumi.
Resource methods are functions attached to specific resource types that return computed values from resources you are managing with Pulumi.
Some managed Kubernetes cluster resources have a resource method to return the generated Kubeconfig file.
Resource methods should be used when you need to get computed values from resources you're managing with Pulumi.
Provider SDKs may include methods attached to a resource type that return computed values from resources managed with Pulumi.
In the Pulumi EKS TypeScript SDK, the Cluster resource's method signature is `getKubeconfig(args?: Cluster.GetKubeconfigArgs): Output<Cluster.GetKubeconfigResult>`.
In the Pulumi EKS C# SDK, the Cluster resource's method signature is `public Output<string> GetKubeconfig(ClusterGetKubeconfigArgs? args = null)`.
In the Pulumi EKS Go SDK, the Cluster resource's method signature is `func (r *Cluster) GetKubeconfig(ctx *Context, args *ClusterGetKubeconfigArgs) (pulumi.StringOutput, error)`.

In the Pulumi EKS Python SDK, the Cluster resource's method signature is `def get_kubeconfig(self, profile_name: Optional[pulumi.Input[str]] = None, role_arn: Optional[pulumi.Input[str]] = None) -> Output[str]`.
Resource methods take `Input` arguments and return an `Output` because they cannot execute until after the resource has been created.
You cannot directly access or manipulate output values using standard language operations like printing or string concatenation.
The `apply` method is typically used for converting inputs to outputs to call `apply` on a value typed as `Input<T>`.
The `apply` method is typically used for accessing nested values in complex types such as outputs that are objects or dictionaries.
For more information about what outputs are and why they are necessary in Pulumi programs, see [Inputs and Outputs](/docs/iac/concepts/inputs-outputs/).
Pulumi provides an `all` method for accessing multiple output values across multiple resources.
Because resources created inside `apply` may not appear in `pulumi preview`, the preview output may not match the actual changes when `pulumi up` is run.
If you pass an output directly as an input to a resource instead of using `apply`, Pulumi will automatically handle the dependency tracking and ensure resources are created in the correct order.
You cannot create stack outputs (using `export` in TypeScript/JavaScript, `pulumi.export()` in Python, `ctx.Export()` in Go, etc.) inside an `apply`.
To use an output value in a YAML program, you reference it directly with interpolation syntax such as `${myResource.myProperty}` and Pulumi resolves the value for you.
The `apply` method does not apply to Pulumi YAML because YAML is a declarative language with no facility for running a function against a resolved value.
YAML is a declarative language with no facility for running a function against a resolved value, so it has no `apply` equivalent.

If you run the program shown with `pulumi up` without using `apply`, you will receive diagnostic output showing the raw Output object representation instead of the resolved value, as illustrated in the per-language CLI output examples.

In C#, calling `[ToString]` on an `[Output<T>]` is not supported, and Pulumi's CLI diagnostic message suggests using `o.Apply(v => $"prefix{v}suffix")` or `Output.Format($"prefix{hostname}suffix")` instead.
See https://www.pulumi.com/docs/concepts/inputs-outputs for more details.

When a Pulumi program is executed with `pulumi up`, the `apply` function will wait for the resource to be created and for its properties to be resolved before printing the desired value of the property.
The Go `ApplyT` function accepts a `T` or `(T, error)` signature, with the latter accommodating error handling.
Go provides an `ApplyTWithContext` function in which the provided context can be used to reject the output as canceled.
The Go function `ApplyT` spawns a Goroutine to await the availability of the implicated dependencies.
Error handling in Go's `apply` may also be achieved using an `error` channel.
AWS Certificate Manager certificate resources can have output properties that are arrays or more complex objects with multiple levels of nested values.
Validating an ACM certificate requires retrieving the value of the resource record from the certificate's domain validation options property, which is an array.
Lifting allows you to access properties and elements directly from a Pulumi Output without needing an `apply`.
When you access a property or array element on an output value in Pulumi, Pulumi automatically lifts that access into the output context, returning a new output that resolves to that nested value.
Lifting nested output access is easier to read and write and does not lose important dependency information needed to properly create and maintain the stack.
Lifting works in most scenarios for accessing nested properties and array elements, but may occasionally cause runtime errors depending on your language.
In TypeScript, if an output resolves to `undefined`, using lifting to reference `outputThatResolvesToUndefined.someProperty` would cause a runtime error.
In Python, the expression `resource.output` results in a call to `resource.__getattr__("output")`, which becomes `resource.apply(lambda r: r.output)`.
In Python, using `hasattr`, which calls `__getattr__` under the hood and looks for an `AttributeError` to determine whether or not a property exists, will not work as expected on resource outputs.
Lifting is currently not supported in Java for Pulumi outputs.
Outputs that return to the engine as strings cannot be used directly in operations such as string concatenation until the output value has returned to Pulumi.
Pulumi's output helpers provide a more concise alternative to calling `apply` directly for the common case of building a string from output values.
Any dependencies of the original output, such as the public DNS property of the server resource, are also kept in the resulting `pulumi.Output<string>` after calling `apply`.
The Pulumi SDK provides helper methods in most languages to make it easier to work with Pulumi outputs and JSON documents.
Pulumi SDK JSON stringify helpers unwrap Pulumi outputs without requiring the use of `apply` and produce JSON string outputs suitable for passing to other resources as inputs.
Amazon S3 bucket policies that apply to objects rather than to the bucket itself require a resource ARN ending in `/*`.
Pulumi provides a parsing helper function that lets you interact with an output in the form of a JSON string like you would a regular JSON object.

In every Pulumi language, an unhandled error raised inside an `apply` callback is reported as a deployment failure, causing `pulumi up` to abort the update and print the error in its diagnostics.
In TypeScript, throwing an exception from the `apply` callback (or returning a rejected promise) rejects the resulting output and fails the update.
In TypeScript, the update fails whether or not the `apply`-derived variable is later used in the program.
In Python, raising an exception from the `apply` callback rejects the resulting output and fails the update.
In Python, the update fails whether or not the `apply`-derived variable is later used in the program.
In Go, the `ApplyT` callback accepts either a `func(T) U` or a `func(T) (U, error)` signature, and returning an error does not panic but rejects the resulting output.
In Go, returning a non-nil error from an `ApplyT` callback does not panic—it rejects the resulting output.
Unlike the other Pulumi languages, Go surfaces a rejected output's error only when the output is consumed—exported as a stack output or passed as an input to another resource.
Go provides `ApplyTWithContext` for cancellation-aware error handling, whose callback receives a `context.Context` that can be used to reject the output when the context is canceled.
In C#, throwing an exception from the `apply` callback rejects the resulting output and fails the update.
In C#, the update fails whether or not the `apply`-derived variable is later used in the program.
In Java, throwing an exception from the `apply` callback rejects the resulting output and fails the update.
In Java, the update fails whether or not the `apply`-derived variable is later used in the program.
To handle a potential apply failure gracefully and continue rather than failing the update, you can catch the error inside the callback and return a fallback value instead of raising.
Resource arguments in Pulumi accept `Input<T>` values, meaning they will take either a plain value or an `Output<T>`.
Component constructors typically accept `Input<T>` parameters to give callers the flexibility to pass either a plain value or an existing output.
The `all` function accepts a mix of plain values and outputs in most Pulumi SDKs.
Pulumi's SDKs provide a dedicated function to wrap any `Input<T>` as a guaranteed `Output<T>`.
In TypeScript, `pulumi.output()` accepts any `Input<T>`—a plain value or an existing `Output<T>`—and returns `Output<T>`.
In Python, `pulumi.Output.from_input()` accepts any `Input[T]`—a plain value or an existing `Output[T]`—and returns `Output[T]`.
In Go, each typed input interface exposes a `ToXxxOutput()` method that returns the corresponding concrete output type; for example, `pulumi.StringInput` provides `ToStringOutput()`.
Each typed input interface in the Go SDK—`pulumi.StringInput`, `pulumi.IntInput`, `pulumi.BoolInput`, and so on—follows the same `ToXxxOutput()` pattern.
In C#, `Input<T>` exposes `Apply` through Pulumi SDK extension methods, so you can often call `Apply` without an explicit conversion step.

When the value passed to Pulumi's Input-to-Output conversion function is already an `Output<T>`, the function returns it unchanged; when passed a plain value, Pulumi wraps it in a new output that resolves immediately with that value.

The stack settings file naming convention is Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml.
The Pulumi stack settings file typically resides in the root of the project directory and stores stack-specific configuration values, secrets metadata, and environment settings.
It is recommended to use the Pulumi CLI commands to edit stack settings files rather than editing them directly, because the CLI commands handle encryption and validation properly.
The stack settings file must be named exactly `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` where `<stack-name>` matches the stack name.
The `encryptedkey` attribute in the stack settings file contains the KMS-encrypted ciphertext for the data key used for secrets encryption, and is only used for cloud-based secrets providers.
The secretsprovider attribute specifies the secrets provider used for encrypting sensitive configuration values.
The encryptedkey attribute contains the KMS-encrypted ciphertext for the data key used for secrets encryption.
The config attribute is a map of configuration key-value pairs for the stack.

The `secretsprovider` attribute's common values include `default` (Pulumi Cloud's default encryption), `passphrase` (a local passphrase for encryption), `awskms://alias/my-key` (AWS KMS), `azurekeyvault://vault-name/key-name` (Azure Key Vault), `gcpkms://projects/my-project/locations/us-central1/keyRings/my-ring/cryptoKeys/my-key` (Google Cloud KMS), and `hashivault://my-secret-path` (HashiCorp Vault).
The secretsprovider attribute specifies which secrets provider to use for encrypting sensitive configuration values.
The secretsprovider value 'awskms://alias/my-key' uses AWS KMS with the specified key.
The encryptedkey field is used when using cloud-based secrets providers like AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or Google Cloud KMS, and contains the encrypted data encryption key.
The `encryptedkey` field is automatically managed by Pulumi and should not be manually edited.
The encryptionsalt field is used when using the passphrase secrets provider and contains the base64-encoded salt used for key derivation.
The `encryptionsalt` field is automatically generated and managed by Pulumi when a user first sets up passphrase encryption.

Configuration keys in the stack settings file's `config` section can be project-namespaced (keys without a namespace, e.g., `name`, `instanceType`) or provider-namespaced (keys with a provider namespace, e.g., `aws:region`, `azure:location`).
Configuration keys in the config section can be project-namespaced, meaning keys without a namespace (e.g., name, instanceType) that belong to the project.

Configuration values in the stack settings file's `config` section can be plain text (string, number, or boolean), encrypted secrets marked with a `secure:` prefix in the YAML, or structured data (complex objects or arrays).
The `environment` section in the stack settings file enables Pulumi ESC (Environments, Secrets, and Configuration) integration.
The `environment` attribute can be a single string naming one environment to import, or an array of strings naming multiple environments to import.
The default stack settings file location can be changed by setting the `stackConfigDir` attribute in the project file to specify a relative directory where stack configuration files should be stored.
When configuration values are set as secrets using `pulumi config set --secret`, they are encrypted in the stack settings file and safe to commit to version control.
It is recommended to check stack settings files into version control for team collaboration, especially for shared environments.
For temporary or ephemeral stacks, users may choose not to commit stack settings files to version control.

The `environment` attribute in a stack settings file supports an inline definition with a `values` key containing structured configuration data such as a `database` object with `host` and `port` fields.
The `pulumi config set --secret` CLI command sets an encrypted configuration value.

All Pulumi IaC resources support a common set of resource options that allow customizing how resources are managed.
Each resource option's reference page describes its behavior in depth and how the Pulumi SDKs enforce which resource types it applies to.
Resource constructors in Pulumi accept a defined set of resource options, each documented on its own reference page describing its behavior and which resource types it applies to.
Resource options that affect provider behavior have no effect on a Pulumi component resource itself, because the component has no backing cloud provider.
The `transforms` option can be used to apply options like `ignoreChanges` to the child resources within a component by modifying child resources as they're created.
When a Pulumi resource option is applied to a component that doesn't support it, the option has no direct effect on the component.
In Pulumi, a child resource does not need to set an inherited resource option itself, because the Pulumi engine carries the value down the parent/child chain at resource registration time.
The Pulumi `envVarMappings` resource option only applies to explicitly configured provider resources.
The Pulumi `parent` resource option defines the parent/child relationship itself rather than being a value that is inherited from a component.
Setting the Pulumi resource options `additionalSecretOutputs`, `deleteBeforeReplace`, or `import` on a component resource is a compile-time error in TypeScript, C#, and Java.
Setting `additionalSecretOutputs`, `deleteBeforeReplace`, or `import` on a component resource is a compile-time error in TypeScript.

For Pulumi resource options that aren't inherited, they must be set individually on each child resource that needs the behavior, or applied via `transforms` on the component to inject the option into matching child registrations as they are created.
The dependsOn resource option specifies additional resource dependencies in addition to those in the dependency graph.
The dependsOn resource option creates a list of explicit dependencies between resources.
Pulumi automatically tracks dependencies between resources when you supply an input argument that came from another resource's output properties.
The dependsOn option ensures that resource creation, update, and deletion operations are executed in the correct order.
Setting dependsOn: [res1] on res2 makes res2 dependent on res1 even if there is no property-level dependency between them.
The dependsOn resource option is available and demonstrated across TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, Java, and YAML.
In TypeScript, passing { dependsOn: [res1] } as a resource option when constructing res2 establishes an explicit dependency on res1.
In Python, passing ResourceOptions(depends_on=[res1]) as the opts argument when constructing res2 establishes an explicit dependency on res1.
In Go, passing pulumi.DependsOn([]pulumi.Resource{res1}) as an option when calling NewMyResource for res2 establishes an explicit dependency on res1.
In C#, setting DependsOn = { res1 } within a CustomResourceOptions object passed to the res2 constructor establishes an explicit dependency on res1.
In Java, calling .dependsOn(res1) on a CustomResourceOptions.builder() used when constructing res2 establishes an explicit dependency on res1.
In a Pulumi YAML program, setting options.dependsOn to a list containing ${res1} under the res2 resource establishes an explicit dependency on res1.
